014768bac0ac: CYMA’s rise to prominence was shaped by one of the most successful partnerships in early Swiss watchmaking. Founded by the Schwob brothers, the company had already established itself as a highly capable manufacturer, recognized for efficiently assembling quality watches from Swiss-made components. A pivotal moment came in 1891 when Henri Sandoz, founder of Tavannes Watch Company, relocated his operations from Le Locle to the village of Tavannes. Sandoz brought with him considerable expertise in complicated watchmaking—particularly repeaters and chronographs—complementing CYMA’s industrial organization and manufacturing strength. What began as a practical collaboration quickly proved mutually advantageous, leading to a formal merger in 1903. In the years that followed, the combined enterprise operated under the names CYMA, Tavannes, and CYMA-Tavannes, reflecting a shared commitment to precision, innovation, and manufacturing excellence. By 1910, the company had become one of Switzerland’s largest watch producers, distinguished by its advanced standardization of parts and remarkably consistent production quality. While Sandoz’s influence reinforced the firm's reputation for sophisticated chronographs, it was the combined technical expertise of both companies that established CYMA and Tavannes as one of the most capable and forward-thinking forces in Swiss watchmaking during the early twentieth century. Then in 1844 Patek met the French watchmaker, Adrien Philippe in Paris where the latter presented his pioneering keyless winding and setting mechanism. Czapek decided to leave the company in 1845 and Adrien Philippe replaced Czapek as Patek’s partner. The company then changed its name to Patek & Cie.before changing once more in 1851 to Patek Philippe & Cie. In 1932, the company was purchased by two brothers Charles and Jean Stern and since then, Patek Philippe S.A. remains a family-owned firm, with the 4th generation at its head. Today, vintage Patek Philippe is a titan in the vintage luxury watch community. c51081da5415: Cartier is a brand that has forever been associated with Opulence, class and sophistication. The company was founded by Louis-François Cartier in 1847 as an ‘ Atelier de Haute Joaillerie ’ after he took over the workshop of his Master, Adolphe Picard. He was succeeded in 1874 by his own son Alfred who continued to uphold the high standards set down by his father. It was not until 25 years later, in 1899 when Alfred’s three sons took over the business and transformed Cartier into a global luxury brand, opening boutiques in London and New York. Cartier’s dalliance with horology started in 1904 when Louis Cartier befriended the aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont. Santos-Dumont complained about the difficulties of checking a pocket watch mid-flight, so Louis Cartier designed a wristwatch with a distinctive flat profile that would henceforth be known as the Cartier Santos-Dumont. This was the first men’s wristwatch made by Cartier and established the foundation of every watch they have produced to this day. It is considered by many to be the pioneer of modern wristwatch design. T akes on classics such as the Tank and Santos Dumont were followed by new designs, including pieces like the Ellipse, the Tonneau, the Ceinture, and more. Today vintage Cartier collectors have the choice of different designs and models from London, Paris and New York houses. Launched in 1959 with the 2998-1; the famous ‘Broad Arrow’ hands of the original reference 2915 Speedmasters were replaced by the far narrower ‘Alpha’ hands to aid legibility. This coupled with the exclusive use of a black printed, external tachymeter scale (initially BASE 1000 but changed to BASE 500 in later models) further enhanced its legibility and cemented the Speedmaster as a world class tool watch. It was to become the first OMEGA in space, as Astronaut Walter ‘Wally’ Schirra would take his own personal 2998-4 On board of the Sigma 7, during the Mercury-Atlas 8 mission (October 1962.) The 2998 is an unusual reference as there are 8 different sub-references produced within a space of only 3 years. The Speedmaster was undergoing constant updates with elements of its design and iconography as well as reference nomenclature being modernised throughout its early production. This has led to each sub-reference having its own particular features which were often updated throughout routine servicing making many watches an assembly of various service replacement parts. This makes finding original, correct examples a challenge to locate and has led the 2998 to become a favourite among collectors. e8ea2089ef1f: The founding of Patek Philippe in 1839 can be traced back to the Polish insurrection of 1830. Taking part in the revolt against Russian rule was a young cavalry officer, Antoine Norbert de Patek who, like many of his compatriots was forced to flee Poland and eventually settle in Geneva. Straight away becoming involved in the city’s watchmaking industry, Patek Czapek & Co was founded with a fellow Pole, François Czapek in 1839. Then in 1844 Patek met the French watchmaker, Adrien Philippe in Paris where the latter presented his pioneering keyless winding and setting mechanism. Czapek decided to leave the company in 1845 and Adrien Philippe replaced Czapek as Patek’s partner. The company then changed its name to Patek & Cie before changing once more in 1851 to Patek Philippe & Cie. In 1932, the company was purchased by two brothers Charles and Jean Stern and since then, Patek Philippe S.A. remains a family-owned firm, with the 4th generation at its head. Today, vintage Patek Philippe is a titan in the vintage luxury watch community. Their obsessive attention to detail combined with ground-breaking feats such as the first serially produced, perpetual calendar wristwatches as well as the first split-second chronograph wristwatch, have made Patek Philippe wristwatches and pocket watches some of the most sought after in the world. 7b876a33f31f: The first Cartier wristwatch — the first sports watch ever made and still an enduring design — the Cartier Santos is one of horology's most significant creations. Yet, it often escapes the recognition it deserves. While beloved by collectors, few fully appreciate the profound influence this watch has had on the industry. The story of the Cartier Santos begins in the early 1900s with the remarkable Alberto Santos-Dumont. Born in 1873 into a family of engineers and farmers, he inherited a spirit of exploration from his father, who worked in railroad construction. That passion soon evolved into his greatest obsession: aviation. After relocating to France, Santos-Dumont designed and piloted balloons, airships, and primitive airplanes, ultimately achieving Europe's first publicly witnessed powered flight. His daring exploits placed him among France's most celebrated figures — including Louis Cartier. Their friendship, grounded in a shared respect for innovation and legacy, inspired Cartier in 1904 to create a watch unlike any before: a square, robust timepiece meant to be worn on the wrist. It was, in essence, the first true sports watch. As radical as Santos-Dumont's flights, the watch defied convention. At a time when pocket watches were the norm, Cartier's bold square wristwatch challenged French tastes. By 1908, the 1904 prototype had evolved into a commercial model, officially launched in 1911. 3256548d44ee: Patek Philippe’s Annual Calendar stands among the most important complications introduced in modern watchmaking. Patented by the manufacture in 1996, it revolutionized the calendar watch by automatically distinguishing between 30- and 31-day months, requiring correction just once each year at the end of February. Elegant in concept and remarkably sophisticated in execution, it remains one of Patek Philippe’s defining innovations. The Ref. 5905 elevates that ingenuity even further by pairing the Annual Calendar with another of the manufacture’s signature complications: the flyback chronograph. Unlike a conventional chronograph, the flyback mechanism allows the timing hand to be reset and immediately restarted with a single press of the pusher—a complication originally developed for pilots and perfectly suited to timing successive intervals with effortless precision. The result is one of the most versatile and technically accomplished watches in Patek Philippe’s contemporary collection. This Ref. 5905P-010, dating to the 2010s, is housed in a commanding 42mm platinum case featuring a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, elegantly sculpted chronograph pushers, and a polished concave bezel. Collectors will also appreciate Patek Philippe's traditional platinum hallmark: a discreet brilliant-cut diamond set into the case band at 6 o'clock, visible only upon closer inspection. 93d9e60b06fa: The late 19th and early 20th centuries were without question the golden age of American watchmaking. The implementation of mass production and interchangeable parts assured American supremacy. Brands such as Gruen, Elgin, and Hamilton vied against the Swiss to dominate the watch industry—and Hamilton, in particular, was at the top of its game. In particular, the development of railroad chronometers gave the manufacture a reputation for accuracy and dependability, in an age where those qualities were vital in a watch. But Hamilton’s production did not rest on railroad chronometers alone: throughout the 1920s and 1930s, and on into World War II, Hamilton released a dizzying array of designs. The brand's aesthetics got more adventurous and polarizing through midcentury and into the 1970s. In 1966, Hamilton was asked to create a prop for the iconic film "2001: A Space Odyssey" by Stanley Kubrick. In 1969, Hamilton did a commemorative edition of the model, changing the name on the dial to the French spelling of Odyssey "Odyssee" to avoid copyright issues. This watch took its mission seriously, embracing the futuristic, otherworldly space climate of the movie's subject line and running with it to generate one of the most exciting watch designs to come from the era. In many ways, this piece predated the space craze of cushion case pieces of the 1970s and comes with an exciting story behind it for lovers of film history. Snag this beauty before someone else does!

b0dbb49fc7d1: There is unusual for Patek Philippe—and then there’s the Reference 5212A-001. At a glance, it reads like a classic Calatrava: clean lines, restrained proportions, and that unmistakable sense of balance that Patek Philippe has spent nearly two centuries perfecting. But look closer, and the 5212A seriousness begins to relax—in the best possible way. Introduced in 2019, this reference brings together a rarely seen complication: the weekly calendar. Alongside the traditional day and date, it tracks the week number, displayed via a central hand against an outer track that corresponds to the months. 42f73936d7b6: The Holy Trinity of watch brands: Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet and Vacheron Constantin. A fantastic blend of retro and contemporary detailing, this watch is not a typical timekeeper, and for that, we love it!
0dd8ea6d1be2: A classic mechanical movement combined with a modern digital display go together like peanut butter and jelly … who would’ve thought? Well, A. Lange & Söhne did when they developed the Zeitwerk in 2009. At the time, the idea of merging a mechanical watch with a digital display was an exciting concept, and in many ways, was ahead of its time — true to the innovative ethos that we’ve come to identify with manufacture hailing from Glashütte . Equipped with a dual-disc mechanism, the Zeitwerk intuitively displays both the hours and minutes through two separate ‘digital’ display windows and is powered by Lange’s patented constant force escapement. Inspired by the renowned five-minute clock perched high above at the Semper Opera House in Dresden and beautifully balanced in its miniaturized execution, the Zeitwerk is a breathtaking example of mechanical art, with a decidedly German flair. This piece - a Reference 140.032 - is a fine example of the first-generation Zeitwerk, and comes housed in a 41.9mm 18K rose gold case featureing a polished bezel, a signed crown at 2 o’clock, a sapphire crystal and a sapphire exhibition caseback that beautifully frames Lange’s manual-winding Calibre L.043.1 movement. Its satin silver dial features a German silver plate housing both jumping hour and minute ‘digital’ displays, a power reserve indicator at 12 o’clock, and a silver-accented constant seconds sub-register at 6 o’clock. Paired to a signed brown alligator leather strap with a signed rose
b4761e87c270: Breguet makes the best dials in the biz. Yeah, we said it. Their signature engine-turned dials, individually numbered and hand-finished, are simply beautiful works of art. The brand also has equally impressive mechanical watchmaking chops to match. Patented in 1801 by Abraham-Louis Breguet, the tourbillon was designed to compensate for the chronometric inaccuracies gravity inflicts on pocket watch movements. In modern times, tourbillons don't have a practical advantage for timekeeping since wristwatches are always being worn in different positions throughout the day, but nonetheless, the tourbillon is a tribute to the quest for accuracy and excellence in fine watchmaking. The Breguet Classique Tourbillon Extra Plat isn’t merely the proud recipient of an excellent Breguet dial, however — it’s also a masterful blend of complicated simplicity. The timekeeping display is executed with blued Breguet hands at the center, a stunning tourbillon cage at 5 o'clock, and power reserve at 8:30. Measuring 41mm in diameter, the piece is an incredibly svelte 7.1mm to wear comfortably and compactly in spite of its complication. The secret? A brilliant slender automatic winding movement, Calibre 581 DR ticking within, measuring just 3mm in thickness. Simply refined on the top; a complicated dance party on the bottom. Dating to the 2020s, this piece is a work of art, displaying an array of beautiful engravings front and back. Stunning to behold and perfectly sized, this Breguet Classique Compli
a3e086277a7c: There are few names in vintage watch collecting that carry the weight of Universal Genève. Long before the modern fascination with luxury sports watches, the Geneva manufacture established itself as one of Switzerland's premier chronograph specialists, producing elegant, technically sophisticated timepieces that remain highly coveted today. The Compax family stands among the brand's greatest achievements and helped define the modern chronograph as we know it. Offered here is a handsome Universal Genève Compax Ref. 52215, presented in a 33mm 14K yellow-gold case and paired with a striking period 'stretch' brick-link bracelet. Elegant without feeling delicate, the watch exemplifies Universal Genève's ability to blend sporting functionality with refined design. The beautifully articulated brick-link construction drapes comfortably on the wrist and is fitted with an uncommon open-end sliding clasp, a thoughtful period detail that speaks to the quality of the watch's original presentation. 0e3bc4d04075: Universal Genève occupies a special place in the history of watchmaking, celebrated for everything from groundbreaking chronographs to some of the most elegant dress watches of the twentieth century. Yet among the manufacture's most charming creations are its jewelry watches—objects that blur the line between timekeeping instrument and wearable sculpture. Offered here is a remarkable yellow-gold brooch watch dating to the mid-century period, showcasing Universal Genève's flair for both design and craftsmanship. Executed in warm yellow gold, the piece centers on a diminutive manually wound watch integrated into a sculptural bow motif. The highly stylized ribbon form reflects the optimism and glamour of postwar jewelry design, with sweeping, architectural folds that transform a familiar decorative element into something distinctly modern. Most fascinating is the orientation of the watch itself. Rather than facing outward in a traditional manner, the dial appears to be suspended upside down above the bow, allowing the wearer to read the time with a simple downward glance. Pinned to a lapel, dress, or jacket, the watch would have been perfectly positioned for discrete time keeping—a thoughtful detail that transforms this decorative jewel into a genuinely practical accessory. The silvered dial is signed Universal Genève and accented by applied indices and elegant dauphine hands, while the compact case provides a subtle counterpoint to the bold sculptural form below. Whether worn a
077f5f3df89d: DOXA's tool watches, particularly of the dive variety, have gained a following among collectors in recent years. We here at Analog/Shift have certainly carried the torch for DOXA's dive watches, and over the years have stocked our inventory (and shamelessly collected for ourselves) exceptional examples of their Sub 300s from the 1960s and 1970s. But while it's DOXA's dive watches that get the most attention, our love for the brand encompasses their whole range of products, rich with impressive timepieces dating to the company's founding. In 1889, Georges Ducommun founded DOXA in that horological hotbed, Le Locle. From the inception of the company, its main stock in trade was dress watches. Their expertly-engineered pocket watches earned a place of distinction with luxury consumers in the early 1900s, and in 1906 DOXA earned a Gold Medal at the International Exhibition in Milan. Throughout the 20th Century, DOXA introduced a wide variety of timepieces. They ranged from consumer grade, time-only watches to ornate ladies cocktail pieces, alarm clocks, precision cockpit instruments (including the first 8-day movement developed for use in automobiles), and military-issued wristwatches. This particular piece is a fantastic representation of the heritage field watch designs that emerged mid-century. A Reference 565, inspired by the Patek 565 Calatrava, this piece features a unique block-like case with the lugs sprouting straight from the midcase. This piece was designed to withstand
126e6f4023e1: What we have here is something truly unique. Made by fine Swiss watchmaker Juvenia, this "Arithmo" calculator watch is one of the coolest watches to come across our desks. Founded in 1860, Juvenia made a variety of beautiful pieces that simply aren't that common these days. The Airthmo is just one example. This piece is unique for its insane calculator functionality hidden under its oversized crystal hanging over the rotating calculator scales. With fixed and rotating slide rules, you can efficiently make precise calculations straight on the wrist. Introduced in the 40s as a practical solution for engineers, in the modern era of smart watches, this was one of the earliest calculator "apps" available for the wrist. If you're on the hunt for a fun vintage piece with loads of history and vintage charm behind it, don't let this beautiful radium-burned dial wind up on the wrist of another and snag this beauty!
0649cc6cd4a9: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, having designed models such as 1942’s Chronomat from the ground as a no-nonsense instrument for use in the cockpit. The Chronomat has evolved significantly since those days, retaining its aeronautical influence but greatly expanding upon its remit to include features such as dive watch-like water resistance and chronometer-grade accuracy. This particular piece, a steel execution likely dating to the early 2000s, features a very wearable, 39mm case with a sapphire crystal, 'fluted' pushers and a matching crown, a timing bezel, and a signed pill bead bracelet. Inside, it has a beautiful rare mother of pearl dial with contrast subsidiary registers, a matching handset, and Breitling's robust and reliable Calibre 13 automatic winding chronograph movement. Beautifully constructed, robust, and perfectly emblematic of a neo-vintgae timepiece from the brand, how can you go wrong?
84c6f6412dad: Few watch brands can compete with Girard-Perregaux in the history department. Dating back to the late 1700's, Girard Perregaux has a story filled with innovation that includes pioneering efforts in early wristwatches and invaluable contributions to the engineering of the quartz movement. Like many other brands, GP worked hard during the 1940’s to build simple, robust watches that could be worn day-to-day, the results of which were myriad beautiful timepieces that can still be had relatively affordably. This particular GP, however, is a modern take on a midcentury aesthetic. This gorgeous Reference 2595 is housed in a 28mm x 44mm rose gold case with a signed crown, a domed sapphire crystal, and an exceptional dial. It features a blacked finished with applique numerals and subsidiary seconds. Although this model dates to the 90s, it certainly feels like a 40s or 50s classic. Powered by a manually wound movement, it preserves the classic historical appeal of these timepieces in a surprisingly modern package. Truly, this is a superlative, gorgeous contemporary dress watch that would make an excellent accent to a suit, or for anyone who enjoys a refined look with casual attire. It walks the line between modernity and vintage appeal, and does so in a truly unique way. This one is a keeper!
60295ee3e69d: There is unusual for Patek Philippe—and then there’s the Reference 5212A-001. At a glance, it reads like a classic Calatrava: clean lines, restrained proportions, and that unmistakable sense of balance that Patek Philippe has spent nearly two centuries perfecting. But look closer, and the 5212A seriousness begins to relax—in the best possible way. Introduced in 2019, this reference brings together a rarely seen complication: the weekly calendar. Alongside the traditional day and date, it tracks the week number, displayed via a central hand against an outer track that corresponds to the months. It’s the kind of function that feels almost academic—until you realize how elegantly it’s been executed. The dial remains airy, legible, and quietly dynamic, a small miracle given the amount of information on display. Then there’s the typography. In a move that feels almost subversive for a brand so rooted in tradition, Patek based the dial text on hand-drawn numerals from the design phase. The result is subtly irregular—each character just slightly different, lending the watch a human touch that’s rare at this level of watchmaking. It’s idiosyncratic, charming, and entirely intentional. Housed in a 40mm stainless steel case—still something of a novelty in Patek’s complicated lineup—the 5212A features stepped lugs, a polished bezel, and a silver opaline dial with blackened gold indices and dauphine hands. Inside, the Caliber 26-330 SC C J SE powers the display with quiet precision, pair
8ca92755bc78: The Patek Philippe Calatrava needs no introduction. Yet every so often, Patek Philippe reminds us that even its most traditional collection can surprise us. The inspiration for the Calatrava Pilot Travel Time can actually be traced back to a little-known chapter of Patek Philippe history. In the 1930s, the manufacture produced a handful of oversized aviator's watches featuring large luminous numerals and highly legible dials for professional use. These rare pieces remained largely forgotten until 2015, when Patek shocked the watch world by introducing the Calatrava Pilot Travel Time Ref. 5524G—a watch that combined vintage aviation aesthetics with one of the brand's most useful modern complications. This particular example, Reference 7234G, distills the formula into a more versatile 37.5mm 18K white gold case. c62e07d06460: In 1991, the soon-to-be graduates at the Geneva School of Engineering were presented with their final project prior to receiving their diploma — to simplify the perpetual calendar. Although the task was easier said than done, their work led to the inception of the annual calendar complication, patented by Patek Philippe in collaboration with the bright engineering minds at the GSE. Five years later, Patek debuted the Reference 5035, a watch powered by the world’s first-ever annual calendar movement and one that finally bridged the gap between a triple-date function and the formidable quantième perpétuel . This slightly later annual calendar, a Reference 5146J, is housed in a beautifully proportioned 39mm 18K yellow gold case with a sapphire crystal, signed crown, and a smooth, polished bezel. This piece packs pedigree, elegance, function and outstanding craftsmanship — exactly what you'd expect from a Patek Philippe!
7f36209d71a7: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brand’s approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design philosophy, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, less-is-more approach to watch design. The Calatrava 96 was also one of the first pieces the brand released after the Stern family purchased a majority share in Patek Philippe in the early 30s. In many respects, the 96 is emblematic of the Stern family’s contributions to Patek. The 96 was one of the earliest round watches Patek ever made, and was also the very first serially produced piece to receive its own reference. In the years since 1932, Patek has released dozens of Calatrava references, each with its own idiosyncrasies. The case features downturned lugs, a polished bezel, a sapphire crystal, a signed crown and an officer-style caseback that when opened, reveals the maison’s Calibre 315 / 190 self-winding movement. Furnished with applied w
0b03766105e2: There was a brief moment in the 1970s when watch design became genuinely experimental. Traditional round cases gave way to bold geometric forms, crystals became sculptural elements, and the line between jewelry, industrial design, and watchmaking began to blur. Few brands embraced this shift more elegantly than Omega, particularly through the influence of celebrated jewelry designer Andrew Grima and the avant-garde design language that emerged from the era. This Omega De Ville 'Emeraude' is a perfect example. Housed in a striking 22mm x 46mm stainless steel case, the watch is less a conventional dress watch than a study in proportion and perspective. Free from unnecessary decoration, the dial feels remarkably modern even half a century later. 0a71d511d597: The future looked different in the 1970s. 4f196933a389: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. A Baignoire on a leather strap is a solid choice for any occasion and has been a favorite at Analog Shift for many years!
5c3e09773278: Few vintage watches have enjoyed a renaissance quite like the Universal Genève Polerouter. This particular Polerouter De Luxe represents one of the most refined expressions of the model. Housed in a beautifully proportioned 34mm 18K rose gold case, it pairs warm precious metal with a wonderfully restrained dial design. 61cafe80cdd6: What you’re looking at is an example of the most important wristwatches of the last 30 years. The Lange 1 is without question the manufacturer’s flagship model, and the big date function is its hallmark. Though found in watches like the Zeitwerk or the Langematik Sax-O-Mat, it’s in the Lange 1 that it’s shown to the greatest effect. Alongside other details such as asymmetrical sub-dials depicting the hours and sub-seconds, and the A. Lange & Söhne signature with its famous ampersand, it shows a clarity of vision that is wholly Lange. e30406cd044a: Vacheron Constantin may be most recognized today for the Overseas collection, but VC has a history that looks way further back than the 70s and the integrated bracelet trend. For the money, it is hard to imagine getting a more unique watch that speaks so characteristically to an important time in the watch industry’s history. ed247470ee64: Few watches have reshaped the modern luxury sports watch landscape quite like the Patek Philippe Aquanaut. 5c43999592ca: Patek Philippe made a fantastic, stainless steel sports watch — and we're not talking about the Aquanaut or the Nautilus. a73db31c8d27: There was a time when watchmakers treated lugs as opportunities rather than necessities. Whether seated beneath the chandeliers of Monte Carlo or holding court at a Las Vegas card table, this is the sort of watch that commands attention without saying a word. The nickname stuck—and one look at the watch explains why. What sets this LeCoultre apart are those remarkable white gold lugs. Sweeping outward from the case in a series of interlocking geometric forms, they create
f74348c1559e: There was a time when every major watchmaker wanted a traveler in its catalog. 0c23828b550a: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t often get the attention they deserve. It seems to be assumed that women are fine with shoddily designed timepieces devoid of soul. Gianni Bulgari, a watch designer and third-generation member of the famed Greek-Italian jewelry dynasty, clearly doesn't feel this way. In 1989, following the sale of his stake in the Bulgari company to his family, he established a new watchmaking firm called GB Enigma in Switzerland to design compelling timepieces with unusual designs. This particular Enigma is an exceptional piece fashioned from stainless steel. Encapsulating exactly the type of design-first mentality that Enigma took in crafting its unique pieces, it features a sapphire cabochon crown and a sapphire crystal. This piece most notably boasts an asymmetrical, almost claw-like case profile unlike anything else on the market, plus a handsome mother-of-pearl dial with a 'dauphine' handset. The red leather strap integrates directly into the case for a seamless flow tied together by a stainless steel deployant clasp, while a handy quartz movement serves as the power plant. For someone on the hunt for a design-forward timepiece to accompany an elegant night at a soirée or gala, it's an ideal choice. And did we mention it comes with its box and papers?

Housed in a 34mm, yellow gold and white gold two tone alternating case with a fantastic, integrated bracelet with a signed clasp, this Polo features a two tone dial with brushed yellow gold components and bands of white gold diamond-set striping. c39d088c64ab: Gianni Bulgari, a watch designer and third-generation member of the famed Greek-Italian jewelry dynasty, feels that women's sports watches should be just as compelling as men's pieces. In 1989, following the sale of his stake in the Bulgari company to his family, he established a new watchmaking firm called GB Enigma in Switzerland to design incredible timepieces with unusual designs. This particular Enigma, an integrated strap sports piece, is emblematic of the firm's bold design philosophy: Housed in a 27mm 18K gold case with an integrated leather strap with matching pin buckle, this piece is completed with a black cabochon crown, a tapisserie dial with applied lume plots a skeletonized 'sword' handset, and a three o'clock date window. All told, this piece would make a great everyday watch. A lesser known brand with a powerful pedigree, an excellent design, and a practical package for everyday applications, don't let this piece slide past you! It's also a great value!
cc19b0539fa9: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, and the original Breitling Chronomat models of 1942 were built from the ground up to be no-nonsense instruments for use in the cockpit. The watch that you're looking at here is a contemporary Chronomat model that is equally no-nonsense! Dating to the 2020s, this Chronomat packs 200 meters of water resistance into the 44mm stainless steel case. Set with a polished steel bi-directional bezel, this piece possesses the classic Breitling case and bracelet paring of world renown. Its matte black dial conveys a plethora of information: An outer tachymeter scale and 1/5th-seconds track are joined by an outsized date window between 4 and 5 o'clock, applied luminous indices, and a triple-register chronograph display with running seconds, 12-hour, and 30-minute registers. A luminous 'sword' handset rounds out the feature set. Powered by the automatic Breitling B01 chronograph movement with a 70 hour power reserve, this hardy tool watch comes paired to its correct stainless steel multi-link bracelet with a signed folding clasp. Happily, it also includes its kit. In need of a serious everyday tool watch that you don't have to baby? Look no further!
4b65c5f551b3: The Reverso is, in essence, one of the very first sports wristwatches. Despite its refined and elegant appearance, it combined utility with a sleek Art Deco exterior that has become an icon of horological design. But in the case of the Reverso, looks deceive. Though the model appears at first glance a dress watch, it owes its existence to the gentlemanly sport of polo. While touring India in the early 1930s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea already taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the problems polo players faced on the field. Once reversed, the delicate components of the case were protected from the shocks sustained while on horseback. No more would polo players crack the crystals or damage the dials of their watches. Chauvot took out a patent for the Reverso in March 1931. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. This particular Reverso, comes in with a 30mm stainless steel reversible case featuring an exhibition caseback on the reverse side. e71d5d242b8a: The IWC Pilot's Watch can trace its history back to the oversized timepieces produced for military aviators in 1940. These enormous pieces were originally designed for maximum legibility in a cockpit setting, and — believe it or not — were meant to be worn on the pilot's thigh! Today, the Pilot's line is perhaps IWC's most identifiable collection, featuring a variety of case and dial configurations suited for any taste — provided your wrist can handle the larger-than-average dimensions. If not, that’s where the Mark series comes in. These watches are contemporary takes on the original Mark X and Mark XI watches from the 1940s. This particular watch, a Pilot's Watch MARK XVI, features a 39mm brushed stainless steel case with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a polished, stepped bezel. It houses a luminous matte black dial with printed ‘Arabic’ indices, a matching ‘sword’ handset, and IWC's Calibre 30110 with 21 jewels and a 41-hour power reserve within. Paired to a beautiful multi-link bracelet, this piece is the essence of a Pilot's watch. With excellent legibility, handsome looks, and utilitarian, military influence, it’s no surprise that the Mark series has become a cornerstone of the IWC collection.
345961d44485: Breitling has long been purveyor of chronographs to pilots, but in the 1950's, the budding popularity of dive watches such as the Rolex Submariner and the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms pushed it to enter that race. In 1957, the brand released both a time-only dive watch, the Superocean Reference 1004, and a chronograph in the form of the Reference 807. These pieces would form the beginning of a long-lasting and ever-evolving line of nautical watches beloved by many. The watch we’re offering here is a tremendously cool, contemporary take on the Superocean that started it all. Housed in an comfortable 36mm case with a polished, white ceramic timing bezel; a signed, screw-down crown; a sapphire crystal; and a signed, blue rubber dive strap with a matching folding clasp, it's a really comfortable everyday companion to add to your collection. The luminous, blue-white dial features quadrant 'baton' markers and 'square' plots with polished surrounds as well as a stylized, luminous handset with a square-tipped seconds hand. Its attention-grabbing attribute, however, lies within a large, white chapter ring that houses a fully graduated minute track. Powered by Breitling’s COSC-certified automatic Caliber 17, this piece is accompanied by its box, travel pouch, hangtag, and card. If you’ve been on the hunt for a robust diver with some everyday appeal, then this Breitling is the answer to your prayers!
f05800904f94: Oftentimes in the hobby of watch collecting, there can be a bit too much focus on what the hot watch of the moment might be - the piece that no one can get, or the watch that everyone wants to own purely so they can say they own it. But in this frenzy of emphasis on what the next big windfall investment piece might be, there are literally tons of watches and brands which slip woefully under the radar. Tissot is among those brands. This particular Tissot is a modern beauty unlike anything else in the price category. A manually-wound skeleton, this piece has no real dial, with a complete openwork look into the industrial movement design architecture. The midcase is brushed, with a brushed bezel and polished case band. It's particularly exciting to see brands like Tissot investing in manually-wound movements. For a modernist look into traditional watchmaking, you'd be hard pressed to beat this piece at the price point! This one will go fast!

Invented and patented by Patek Philippe in the 1990s, it elegantly bridges the gap between simple calendar watches and their more complex perpetual counterparts. Accounting for months of varying lengths, it requires correction just once a year, at the end of February — a small marvel of mechanical logic disguised as everyday convenience. But this is no ordinary annual calendar. The Reference 5905P-001 pairs that ingenuity with a flyback chronograph, allowing the wearer to reset and restart the timing function with a single push. It’s a complication born from utility — timing laps, intervals, moments that matter — yet here it’s executed with the kind of refinement only Patek can deliver. The result is a watch that feels as technically accomplished as it is visually composed. Housed in a 42mm platinum case, this example features a rich blue dial that shifts beautifully in the light, anchored by applied indices and a crisp white minute track framing the chronograph register. The layout is classic Patek: day, date, and month displayed across the top, with a running seconds indication subtly integrated above six. The luminous obelisk hands complete the look, balancing legibility with elegance. 8288dee78819: There’s a certain confidence in a watch that doesn’t need to reinvent the wheel — it simply refines it. The Girard-Perregaux Laureato has long occupied that sweet spot between sport and sophistication, a design born in the 1970s that remains as relevant today as it was at its inception. Its signature architecture — the interplay between a round case and octagonal bezel, paired with a seamlessly integrated bracelet — remains one of the most quietly compelling shapes in modern watchmaking. This contemporary Laureato Chronograph, Reference 81020-11-431-11A, leans into that legacy with a crisp, steel execution and a striking blue dial. Housed in a 42mm stainless steel case with a domed bezel and screw-down crown, it offers a reassuring sense of solidity on the wrist. Powered by a Swiss automatic movement and water resistant to 100 meters, this is a watch built for daily wear — equally at home under a cuff or out in the world. The integrated steel bracelet with folding clasp completes the package, reinforcing that fluid, cohesive feel that defines the Laureato line. Sporty, architectural, and effortlessly wearable, it’s a modern classic that knows exactly what it is, and doesn’t try too hard to be anything
9b721b80c61f: There is perhaps no more versatile complication than the chronograph. From race cars to rocket ships, boats to battlefields, you are likely to find a chronograph being employed to measure a plethora of tasks and times. From the Greek khrónos (“time) and gráphō (“to write”), a chronograph is a watch that has the ability to record time, generally via the addition of small sub-counters that register minutes and hours. Though many storied brands produced notable chronographs during the complication’s heyday from the 1930s through the 1970s, numerous other firms fell by the wayside during the Quartz Crisis, folding completely and disappearing or being rolled up into conglomerates that pillaged their stores of parts. Heuer, for its part, is still around today as TAG Heuer, but its pre-TAG period was perhaps its most fertile era of chronograph design. Take the Calculator watch, for example: this special model took advantage of the brand's esteemed automatic chronograph movement technology and paired it with a unique two-part slide rule bezel in what can best be described as a sort of mechanical calculator: Using the bezel, the wearer can easily calculate distance and weight and convert between metric and imperial. Pretty neat! This particular Heuer Calculator watch, a Reference 110.633, dates to the 1970s and features a 45.5mm 'tonneau-shaped' stainless steel case with an outer calculator bezel, dual 'pump' pushers, a left-hand crown, and a stainless steel multi-link bracelet. ade061f7ed0d: Seiko makes fantastic watches. Pure and simple. From the rare as hen's teeth Hi-Beat 6159 to the film-famous 6105 and 6309 models to the economy workhorse SXK007, Japanese watchmakers perfected incredibly well-made tool watches decades ago - and at prices that make the most diehard Swiss watch fans question their spending habits. This piece, a Reference SRQ057 , dates to 2025 and recalls one of the coolest pieces of Seiko history. In 1971, a Seiko Datsun was on the wrist of number 11 when he won the East-African Safari Rally, one of the most harrowing races in history. The incredible chrono we have here is a tribute limited edition of the Datsun, sporting the advantages of modern watchmaking including sapphire crystals and an updated automatic movement. The piece measures 42mm in diameter and features an automatic movement within. Built on a reputation for fine chronograph construction, this Seiko is one to save for the ages, recalling one of the coolest moves in Seiko history. These are wonderful timepieces that represent just about everything that we love about Seiko and are overlooked by many. Don't make that mistake!
12a5d263aef8: In the 1950s and 1960s, the cocktail watch wasn’t just an accessory, it was part of the occasion. These pieces were designed to disappear into the rhythm of an evening, catching light rather than attention, pairing effortlessly with silk, champagne, and late hours. Small in scale but often extravagant in execution, they balanced mechanical ingenuity with jewelry-level artistry in a way that feels increasingly rare today. This particular example from Lucien Piccard captures that spirit beautifully. Founded in 1923 in Lausanne, the brand built its reputation on elegant, refined dress watches, and this piece leans fully into that heritage. The petite dial sits almost like a secret at the center of a fully diamond-set case, framed by brilliant stones that extend seamlessly into a 'tennis' style bracelet. Tapered 'baguette' accents add structure and geometry, giving the piece just enough architectural edge to balance the sparkle. Look closer, and the charm deepens. The signed crown features Piccard’s signature flourish — a subtle, almost whimsical curlicue that feels delightfully out of step with the otherwise formal design. It’s a small detail, but exactly the kind that gives a watch personality. Finished with a box clasp and safety latch, the diamond 'tennis' style bracelet wears as fluidly as it looks. Light, intricate, and undeniably glamorous, it’s a reminder of a time when watches were made not just to tell time, but to celebrate it.

Founded in 1775 by Abraham-Louis Breguet, the maison is responsible for some of the most important inventions in watchmaking history, including the tourbillon, the Breguet overcoil, and the 'pare-chute' shock protection system. Just as influential, however, is the brand’s design vocabulary: engine-turned guilloché dials, elegant 'Roman' numerals, and those unmistakable blued 'Breguet' hands. These weren’t just aesthetic choices — they were innovations in legibility and refinement, developed for an elite clientele that included royalty, scientists, and statesmen. That balance of technical mastery and visual restraint remains at the core of Breguet today. This Ladies’ Classique Ref. 8561 is a perfect expression of that enduring philosophy. Crafted in 18K white gold, the 25.5mm case is elegantly framed by a diamond-set bezel and lugs, adding brilliance without disrupting the watch’s elegance. Beneath the sapphire crystal sits Breguet’s signature silvered guilloché dial that is engine-turned by hand, individually finished, and endlessly captivating as it plays with the light. Blued steel hands sweep across 'Roman' numerals with that unmistakable Breguet grace, while a signed crown, marked with the maison’s “B,” completes the overall design. 186cdbb07185: Patek Philippe may be known for its complicated calendar watches, but it’s equally renowned for the simple, elegant dress watches it makes for both men and women. Take the Twenty-4 line, for example: Released in 1999, this ladies’ collection is geared toward the modern women in search of a superlative timepiece that oozes elegance and class. Available in rectangular and round case profiles in various metals and configurations, it’s one of the best dedicated women’s watch collections on the market today. This particular Twenty-4, a Reference 4910/20G-011 from circa 2004, is a quietly expressive take on one of Patek Philippe’s most enduring designs. Housed in a 25mm rectangular case, it features polished brancards set with two elegant rows of diamonds, framing a soft cream dial with a matching handset. A Calatrava-signed crown and integrated multi-link bracelet complete the look, balancing refinement with everyday wearability. In great condition, showing light wear and powered by a reliable quartz E15 movement, this is a stunning timepiece that has to be seen to be believed.
902369cc1b2a: Patek Philippe has long been known for its complicated watchmaking, but following the stock market crash of 1929, fewer clients had the means to purchase these high-end timepieces. After securing a controlling interest in the firm, Jean and Charles Henri Stern decided to create a simple watch that would come in at a lower price point and appeal to the firm’s clientele. Using the principles espoused by the Bauhaus school and its minimalist, function-first philosophy, Patek conceived the Calatrava, taking its name from the Spanish military order established in the 12th century which had become the symbol of Patek Philippe. Since its debut in 1932, the Calatrava has become a byword for a simple, time-only dress watch — even from brands other than Patek itself. This piece, a Reference 6119G-001, builds on the foundational designs of its three-hand predecessors and is housed in a 39mm white gold case with a guilloché Clous de Paris bezel, signed crown, a sapphire crystal and a svelte case profile that will delight any wrist. The dial features a dynamic, vertically satin brushed anthracite tone acting as a canvas for its applied gold indices, the constant-seconds subsidiary register at 6 o’clock, a 'dauphine' handset and a white-accented ‘railroad’ minute track Powered and visible by way of a sapphire exhibition caseback, this Calatrava features a hand-wound Patek Philippe Calibre 30-255 PS and comes fitted to a signed black alligator leather strap with a signed 18K white gold pin

The Reference 5060J, launched in 1996 for the 20th anniversary of the Nautilus, was a sort of transitional watch. Borrowing features from the Nautilus but doing away with the famed case “ears” of that porthole-inspired model and adding lugs, it provided the basis for the Reference 5060A in 1997, the first model actually bearing the Aquanaut name. The Aquanaut would go on to form the basis of a full collection of luxury sports watches that provided the entry point into the Patek Philippe catalog. This piece, a Reference 5167/1A-001, dates to 2016 and features a 40mm stainless steel case with a satin-finished bezel, sapphire crystal, a signed screw-down crown and a water resistance rating up to 120 meters. On the dial you'll find all of the signature Aquanaut features present — offered in an ombre anthracite tone that fades to black towards the edges, 'hobnail' texturing, luminous Arabic indices, a matching luminous handset and a date indicator at 3 o’clock. In excellent condition throughout and fitted to a black rubber strap with a signed steel button-deployant clasp, this piece is accompanied by all of its factory goodies including its inner and outer box set, signed leather folio, and a Certificate of Origin, alongside the signed steel multi-link bracelet it was originally sold with. de93c9068174: There’s a particular kind of confidence in doing less, and doing it exceptionally well. Longines has long understood this balance, and pieces like this are a perfect expression of that restraint. Rather than relying on ornament or complication, it leans fully into proportion, surface, and line — the quiet fundamentals that define truly enduring design. Housed in an elongated rectangular 18K yellow gold case, this ultra-slim “Tank” silhouette feels almost architectural on the wrist. The brushed gold dial continues that theme, stripped down to its essence with only a subtle 'crosshair' layout and a simple handset. No numerals, no excess — just a study in symmetry and tone that shifts beautifully with the light. Powered by a manual-wind movement, it stays true to traditional watchmaking while maintaining an almost jewelry-like presence. Paired with a rose-colored alligator strap, the warmth of the gold case is amplified, giving the watch an understated yet unmistakably elegant character.
aaeb7dc60a87: There was a moment in the late 1960s when the Swiss watch industry hit reset. The 1969 introduction of the Seiko Astron — the world’s first commercially available quartz wristwatch — sent real tremors through traditional watchmaking. In response, a consortium of major Swiss brands, including Patek Philippe, Rolex, Omega, and Piaget, joined forces to develop their own answer: the Beta 21. Introduced that same year, it was an ambitious electronic caliber, featuring a quartz crystal oscillating at 8,192 Hz, reduced to drive a vibration motor with a smooth, sweeping seconds hand — a detail that set it apart from the “tick” we now associate with quartz. Despite enormous investment, only around 6,000 movements were produced before the project was ultimately abandoned, making surviving examples all the more compelling today. This Piaget reference 14101, dating to around 1970, captures that moment of experimentation and uncertainty with remarkable clarity. Powered by the Beta 21, it’s as much a piece of horological history as it is a wristwatch. The solid 18K yellow gold “Jumbo” case — measuring approximately 40mm by 33.5mm — embraces the scale of the movement with confidence. Its stepped construction and softly rounded rectangular form give it a distinctly sculptural presence, while the black dial, framed by a subtle inner track and accented with gold markers and 'baton' hands, keeps the overall composition clean and intentional. 764920d77580: Few names in Swiss watchmaking carry the quiet authority of Girard-Perregaux. c8756629f6b7: The Reverso, Jaeger-LeCoultre's most distinctive watch, certainly has an impressive pedigree. While touring India in the 1920s, Swiss businessman César de Trey met a British polo player who'd just cracked the crystal of his watch on the field. De Trey returned to Switzerland with an idea that had taken root in his head, which he then discussed with Jacques-David LeCoultre: What if a watch could be made with a case that could reverse? The reversible case, masterminded by designer Alfred Chauvot, was Jaeger-LeCoultre's solution to the impact problem polo players could face on the field. Produced chiefly in steel, Jaeger-LeCoultre also released the Reverso in gold, and decorated the case back with engravings or even miniature portraits. 195ef172781c: The story of Bulova is deeply entwined with American manufacturing. Its founder, a Czech immigrant named Joseph Bulova, was inspired by the advances that Ford made in his factory in Highland Park, Michigan. Starting in 1912, Bulova built a factory in Biel, Switzerland, using Ford’s principles of mass production. The brand was among the first to offer a wide range of wristwatches for men, with a distinctive visual style that—thanks to its innovative adoption of advertising and a relocation to Astoria, Queens—became fixed in the American imagination. Bulova took over offices in the Empire State Building and installed an observatory on the roof, in order to measure universal time. In the workshop down below, watchmakers timed the watches they were working on to readings taken in the observatory. The watches that Bulova produced were varied, from handsome three-handers to divers and even chronographs. This particular piece, a Reference A-17 dates to the 1950s. The A-17 was produced for the US military initially, this piece a 'civilian' example. Measuring in at 32mm and sporting a 10BNCH manually wound movement, this piece has a classic military aesthetic with a beautiful charcoal dial with incredibly legible indexes in excellent condition. Whether you're a seasoned collector or just getting started, it's hard to go wrong with a timelessly designed manually-wound watch with a military history. And lets face it, wearing a nearly 100 year-old watch is just cool.

Freed from convention, he pursued bold shapes and sculptural forms that felt more like jewelry with a pulse than traditional timepieces. It’s not delicate in the predictable sense. It’s assertive. Distinct. Glamorous without being obvious, this is the kind of watch that refuses to blend in.

e06c140c12f8: There’s something quietly compelling about a watch that marks a turning point. The Movado Tempo-Matic, traces its roots to one of the brand’s most important technical milestones. b4ccdc3c94eb: The 1970s were not a timid decade — and neither is this Tissot. This Seastar Navigator Chronograph captures that era’s confidence in full color. 20648ae751ab: Watches have been indispensable tools for explorers since John Harrison created his marine chronometer in the 1760s, even as more sophisticated technologies like radar emerged in the 20th century. But none of this could have happened without John Harrison’s chronometer; before he developed it in the 1760s, successful navigation was more a product of luck than science. The problem wasn’t latitude, but longitude. Navigators could determine their latitude by the angle of the sun at noon, or that of Polaris—the North Star—at twilight. But the rolling motion of a ship at sea rendered that method impossible when it came to determining longitude. Although scientists suggested using an accurate clock—or chronometer—for that purpose as early as the 1500s, early attempts proved insufficient when faced with the endless undulation of the ocean. This problem would prove deadly in 1707, when a fleet of four warships floundered on the rocks surrounding the Isles of Scilly. Squalls and gales had blown the ships off course, and due to the inability of the fleet’s navigators to determine their position, they assumed that they were off the coast of France. Jorgen's son, Urban, followed in his father's footsteps, studying below some of the best watchmakers of the era in Switzerland, Paris and London. By the time Jules was born in 1808, the family name was enmeshed with clock and watchmaking. Jules furthered the prestige by designing and achieving patents that became benchmarks of style and function for pocket watches, so much so that they were incorporated into many American pocket watches right through to the late 1800s. The Jurgensen name continued to resonate throughout Europe well into the mid-1900s, despite having been sold to an American company in the late 1930s. 9c0ff26e2db3: The Annual Calendar is a complication invented by Patek Philippe . This particular example, a 5205G-013, is a successor to the 5035, with a few additional refinements. Coming in at 40mm in diameter, this piece features a lovely, solid 18K white gold case with hollowed lugs; a polished, concave bezel; a signed crown; a sapphire crystal; a sunburst blue 'sector' dial with day, date, month, and moonphase apertures; applied faceted 'baton' indices and a matching 'dauphine' handset. dc6c173995af: We’re known for our love of DOXA Subs. In any flavor, any color — from the classic, orange-dialed Professional to the stunning silver-dialed Searambler — we love 'em all. In fact, the original inspiration behind Analog:Shift was squarely centered on DOXA! In such a way, elegance was not substituted for functionality, and the De Ville could be worn with a suit and not lose any of its water resistance. As time progressed, so too did the spec sheet of the average De Ville become more impressive, leading to a collection of handsome yet robust timepieces perfect for everyday wear. The particular De Ville we have here is a modern incarnation from the 2020s boasting a simple, elegant design that can truly be dressed up or down with ease. Housed in a 28mm two tone case in rose gold and stainless steel, this piece is fitted with a sapphire crystal, a signed crown, and a diamond-set bezel, it features a butterfly motif champagne dial with applied Roman and diamond indices, and a ‘dauphine’ handset. Powering the watch is the quartz Omega Calibre 1376 movement. Whether your needs are for an everyday timepiece or a watch for special occasions, you can’t go wrong with this versatile De Ville and its chronometer-certified movement. Give it a whirl and see what we mean! It has all the ingredients of a perfect dress watch.

f9e1a8e97142: The panther holds a special place in the history of the world’s most famous jeweler. During the First World War, the Parisian maison designed a ladies’ wristwatch with a spotted diamond and onyx pattern. Commissioned by Louis Cartier, it was a gift to Belgian-French jeweler Jeanne Toussaint, whom he referred to as ‘ La Panthère .’ Over a century later, the Panthère line is still a fixture in the Cartier catalog, and the big cat motif appears frequently on watches, jewelry, and more. This particular Panthère de Cartier is a ladies’ wristwatch in the brand’s 'mini’ size. Housed in a 17mm x 23mm white gold case, a sapphire crystal, and a stepped, smooth bezel with decorative rivets and diamond settings, it features a silver Roman dial and a matching blued-steel ‘sword’ handset. Powered by a quartz movement and paired to a matching, white gold multi-link bracelet, this svelte wristwatch is the very essence of Cartier: beautiful, elegant, and lasting. Whether you wear this special piece as an accent to eveningwear or as an everyday watch, the Panthere in white gold is surely suitable.
94e5a0a594f8: First presented in 1932 with the Reference 96, the Patek Philippe Calatrava is the benchmark for classic men’s dress watches. The groundbreaking reference set the stage for nearly every piece Patek has released since, and became the blueprint for other brands' approaches to classy men’s timepieces. Heavily influenced by the Bauhaus design movement, the Calatrava was then considered extremely modern with its minimalist, ‘less is more’ approach to watch design. In point of fact, it's still considered extremely modern. In the years since 1932, Patek has released dozens of Calatrava references, each with its own idiosyncrasies. Almost all share the underlying DNA of the 96, prioritizing subtle elegance above all else. The recently released Reference 6119 blends details from many different past Calatravas to splendid effect: The hobnail bezel of the 3919, the case profile of the Reference 96, the indices of the 5196, and a brand new, manually-wound movement designed specifically for this reference with an improved 65-hour power reserve fueled by a double barrel are all present. Housed in a larger 39mm case, it feels like a distinctly contemporary watch inspired by Patek's storied watchmaking past. This Reference 6119, presented in 18K rose gold, comes with a silver dial that generates a warm hue with interplay from a brown leather Patek Philippe strap with a rose gold pin buckle. 70ccfd23f621: Cartier's Tank is one of the icons of the watch industry. Over its history, it has gone through a whole host of unique iterations with their own unique personalities. Perhaps no model has as distinctive a look as the coveted Tank a Guichets. Notably released in 1928 and worn by jazz icon Duke Ellington, the watch is strikingly recognizable thanks to its jump hour display. Carved into a slab of red gold, this watch truly embodies the 'tank' aesthetic of its namesake. Cut into the surface of the slab of gold is a unique jump hour display, flaunting the hours in a window at 12, and the minutes on a radial display at 6 o'clock. Over the history of the Tank à Guichets since 1928, very few examples have actually been made. Several piece uniques were introduced in the early to mid 20th century. Then, in 1997, the brand did a 150 piece limited edition in platinum. Next, we get to this piece, part of the coveted Cartier CPCP collection limited edition of 100 pieces in 2005. What you're looking at is a truly rare icon in the Cartier collections. Don't pass up this opportunity, it doesn't come up often. When the top of the hour comes, you'll find yourself taking a moment out of your day to watch the disc jump from one to the next. In short, this is a special one.

Since then, Bell & Ross has expanded into different case shapes and design profiles — but the square BR-01’s evolution, the BR-03, remains a mainstay in the catalog. This particular BR-03 is a Reference BR0394-SW-CE/SRB from the 2020s. Housed in a 42mm black ceramic case with a sapphire crystal and a signed crown, it features a luminous dial with a multi-scale chronograph display, and a matching handset. Absurdly legible and boasting military-inspired cool, it’s powered by a Swiss-made BR-CAL.301 movement and comes paired to a rubber strap with a PVD coated stainless steel pin buckle. In mint condition, and including its factory goodies, this masterpiece of utilitarian design is an excellent entry point into the world of Bell & Ross, and into the realm of military-inspired design in general. Try it on for yourself!

e1bbc62a0aa1: There is perhaps no more versatile complication than the chronograph. From race cars to rocket ships, boats to battlefields, you are likely to find a chronograph being employed to measure a plethora of tasks and times. From the Greek khrónos (“time) and gráphō (“to write”), a chronograph is a watch that has the ability to record time, generally via the addition of small sub-counters that register minutes and hours. Though many storied brands produced notable chronographs during the complication’s heyday from the 1930s through the 1970s, numerous other firms fell by the wayside during the Quartz Crisis, folding completely and disappearing or being rolled up into conglomerates that pillaged their stores of parts. Heuer, for its part, is still around today as TAG Heuer, but its pre-TAG period was perhaps its most fertile era of chronograph design. Take the Calculator watch, for example: this special model took advantage of the brand's esteemed automatic chronograph movement technology and paired it with a unique two-part slide rule bezel in what can best be described as a sort of mechanical calculator: Using the bezel, the wearer can easily calculate distance and weight and convert between metric and imperial. Pretty neat! This particular Heuer Calculator watch, a Reference 110.633, dates to the 1970s and features a 45.5mm tonneau-shaped stainless steel case with an outer calculator bezel, dual pump pushers, a left-hand crown, and a stainless steel multi-link bracelet. 7224507ecb96: What is it about vintage watches that gets our heart racing? Sometimes it’s the quaint aesthetic, beautiful patina, or the history they represents that tugs at our heartstrings. At other times, it’s the untold stories imbued into each and every mark, scuff and scratch that gives a timepiece that undeniable charm we so desperately love. This time-only Elgin from the 1940s is imbued with precisely this type of character. Housed in a quaint gold case, this small-but-mighty piece features an acrylic crystal, an signed crown, elongated lugs, and an engraved caseback that commends a Mr. Barnett for 20 years at Firestone Service — always read the caseback, as they say! The dial has patinated to an awesome champagne tone and applied indices, a matching sharp handset, central-seconds hand . Outfitted with a thin leather strap with a matching gold buckle, this piece is powered by a self-winding Elgin 25 jewel movement. Some say that small watches are back. We say they never left!

Furthermore, this one has U.S. Navy provenance as evidenced by en engraved caseback. Dating from the late 1960s, the Tudor Subs featuring the early Rose logo are very similar to their Rolex 5513 cousins, yet are considerably rare due to a smaller production run. ee7a80522427: Seiko makes fantastic watches. Pure and simple. From the rare as hen's teeth Hi-Beat 6159 to the film-famous 6105 and 6309 models to the economy workhorse SXK007, Japanese watchmakers perfected incredibly well-made tool watches decades ago - and at prices that make the most diehard Swiss watch fans question their spending habits. This piece, a Reference 7017-6040, dates to circa 1970s and features a 40mm stainless steel round case with hooded lugs, a matte dark dial with day date functionality framed at 3 o'clock, this piece is topped off with an orange chronograph hand for timing short interval events. With a very funky period-style and excellent functionality, it's not hard to see why these 1970s Seiko chronographs are developing a cult following. These are wonderful timepieces that represent just about everything that we love about vintage and are overlooked by many. Don't make that mistake!
0b8359bd0e17: No, it’s not a Tank. And yes, it deserves your attention! While Parisian jeweler to the stars Cartier may be best known in horological circles for its famed Tank watch, the French firm produced — and continues to produce — numerous other watch models that deserve equal billing for their unique and sumptuous designs . The Louis Cartier collection, announced by Cartier Paris in 1973, constituted a redesign of the maison’s watch offerings upon its launch. Fresh takes on classics such as the Tank and Santos Dumont were accompanied by new designs, including that of the Ellipse. A slim, horizontal watch with a simple “Roman” dial, the Ellipse conveys the same spectacular design principles as the Tank in an unconventional format. This particular Ellipse features a beautiful 32mm yellow gold case with factory onyx and diamond inlays, Cartier's signature cabochon winding crown, and its centerpiece white “Roman” Paris-signed dial with blued steel sword hands and 'railroad' minute track. Paired to a black leather strap with a matching 18k yellow gold deployant clasp, this piece makes for a beautiful dress watch — or a daily driver! Everyone knows the Tank. This is your chance to own its equally compelling sibling!

ebd55f2c466e: Ladies' watches, unfortunately, don’t get the attention they deserve. It seems to be assumed that women are fine with shoddily designed timepieces devoid of soul. Of course, this is nonsense — there’s no reason whatsoever that a lady’s watch should be any less considered than a man’s! Bulgari is one of few companies whose thoughtful ladies’ watches have risen to the top — perhaps because of the firm’s background as a jeweler. The Serpenti, a serpentine collection of womens's timepiece that originated in the aftermath of World War II, is today an iconic masterpiece of industrial design. e709e284834a: Never heard of a ‘Super Compressor’ before? e3ffa1a9cd9c: Baume & Mercier hasn't traditionally gotten a lot of attention from the watch collector elite, and that's OK — they may not be the most exclusive, in-demand watches of the moment, but they pack a lot of punch for their weight class, and offer a tremendous value for the enthusiast-minded! c1a52e4d2aa8: Despite being a relatively modern wristwatch, the IWC Aquatimer Reference 3536 has a storied history. 2c4dd36aaf30: The Rolex Sea-Dweller was introduced in 1967 as the ultimate tool watch for professional saturation divers. During the 1960s, commercial divers working on pioneering saturation diving projects—such as France's COMEX and the U.S. Navy's SEALAB program—spent days living and working inside pressurised underwater habitats while breathing a helium-rich gas mixture known as Heliox. Because helium molecules are exceptionally small, they could penetrate the watch's rubber gaskets and accumulate inside the case. During decompression, the trapped helium expanded faster than it could escape, creating enough internal pressure to force the acrylic crystal from the watch. To solve this problem, Rolex co-developed and patented the Helium Escape Valve (HEV). Positioned at 9 o'clock on the case, this ingenious one-way valve automatically releases excess helium once the internal pressure reaches a critical level, preventing damage to the crystal and ensuring the watch remains watertight and fully functional. 8e7d54548671: Since its official debut in 1956, the Day-Date has been produced exclusively in precious metals. As the flagship model of the Genevan manufacturer, it has long been synonymous with success, frequently seen on the wrists of heads of state, royalty, and other influential figures. Most Day-Dates were fitted with discreet, conservative dials—after all, most buyers of this model preferred elegance over extravagance. But Rolex made a notable exception to this unwritten rule: beginning in the 1970s, they introduced bright, high-gloss lacquered dials known today as “Stella” dials. At the time, these bold colours were not widely embraced, precisely because they attracted attention. As a result, production numbers remained low, making them highly sought after today. A wide array of colours is known—yellow, green, orange, red ,pink and multiple shades of blue, some embellished with gemstones, and produced across different metals. They also span various generations: from the early 18xx “pie-pan” versions to the later 18xxx models with flat dials. The manufacturing process was exceptionally labor-intensive. Each dial was spray-painted and then oven-baked to set the pigment. This cycle was repeated multiple times until the desired depth of colour and finish was achieved. Afterward, the dial was polished and coated with a clear lacquer. This final step created the distinctive effect where the printed text appears to float above the glossy surface, reminiscent of the porcelain-dial Daytonas.

The dial is built in layers, a central onyx disc, a string of brilliant diamonds around it, then an outer ring of onyx framing the whole thing. 41bf30985b55: Lo Speedmaster nasce nel 1957. Due anni dopo, nel ’59, Omega realizzò la seconda generazione della famiglia di orologi, con lo stesso movimento della precedente – il mitico calibro 321 – ma con delle modifiche evidenti : le lancette Lollipop al posto di quelle Broad Arrow e la lunetta con la scala tachimetrica in alluminio nero e non più in acciaio. Proprio di questo modello si innamorò Walter Schirra – Wally, per gli amici – pilota della US Navy che acquistò lo Speedmaster CK 2998 in una gioielleria di Houston, qualche mese prima di partire per lo Spazio come pilota titolare della missione Mercury-Atlas 8, lanciata da Cape Canaveral il 3 ottobre 1962, a bordo della capsula Sigma 7. Durante quelle 9 ore e passa di volo, aveva al polso il suo Speedmaster. Lo aveva indossato a titolo personale, con l’intenzione di utilizzarlo come back-up per l’orologio di bordo. Anche se non fu una scelta ufficiale dell’agenzia spaziale, il CK 2998 funzionò perfettamente. Divenne così, di fatto, il primo Omega nello spazio e inaugurò la serie di esemplari utilizzati – poi su protocollo Nasa – per le esplorazioni spaziali. Questo bellissimo esemplare è in particolare una referenza 2998-3, perfettamente coevo in ogni sua componente e caratterizzato da una piacevolissima e calda patina del tempo. Completo della sua scatola originale e del suo tag! fa12ccd1eb05: Bellissimo Rolex Ref. 6062 con liconico quadrante con indici a stella, dal quale prende il soprannome di “Stelline”. Questo è probabilmente il Rolex più iconico mai prodotto e, dato il suo breve periodo di produzione (1950 1953 circa), è oggi un modello estremamente raro e ricercato. Nel secondo dopo-guerra, verso la fine degli anni 40, lindustria orologera attraversò un periodo di forte crisi dettata soprattutto dalla difficoltà nellesportare le merci a cui conseguì una forta diminuzione del fatturato. Rolex decise di impiegare i migliori mastri orologiai nello sviluppo di nuove meccaniche sofisticate. Il design conosciuto dei vecchi Datejust e Bubbleback, forte della ormai collaudata cassa Oyster, abbracciò le nuove meccaniche su base cal. 655, per dare vita a un nuovo modello decisamente più sofisticato, con indicazione di un triplo calendario con fasi lunari, una novità assoluta per Rolex! Tuttavia, Rolex cessò presto la produzione di questa referenza, concentrandosi piuttosto sugli orologi-strumento (per lo più in acciaio) come lExplorer (1953), il Submariner (1953), il GMT (1955), ecc. Ci sono voluti più di 70 anni per rivedere un calendario con fasi lunari nella collezione Cellini contemporanea. Malgrado il fondello avvitato, limpermeabilità di questo modello era precaria ed è il motivo per cui molti quadranti si rovinarono con il passare degli anni. Ingenuamente molti di essi furono restaurati in tempi più moderni, impattando negativamente sulloriginalità e il valore

6d5d208279b0: Lo storico e raro Blancpain Fifty Fathoms No Radiation Diver degli anni 60! E stato il primo orologio da polso con lunetta girevole e movimento automatico. Lanciato nel 1953 in collaborazione con lélite dei sommozzatori francesi, Lunità militare aveva bisogno di un orologio da polso affidabile, durevole, leggibile e resistente allacqua. Per coincidenza, lamministratore delegato di Blancpain, Jean-Jacques Fiechter, aveva una grande passione per le immersioni e accettò subito la sfida. Questi primi orologi Fifty Fathoms erano dotati inizialmente di luminescenza al radio, che permetteva di ottenere un bagliore costante in ambienti bui per aiutare la leggibilità. Il Blancpain Fifty Fathoms, soprannominato “No Rad”, risale ai primi anni 60 ed è forse uno degli orologi subacquei depoca più collezionabili! Ciò è dovuto al grande simbolo “No Radiations” che si trova nella metà inferiore del quadrante. Si scoprì infatti che il radio utilizzato per la luminescenza dei primi orologi da polso aveva proprietà distruttive per il corpo umano e molti marchi si convertirono rapidamente al trizio, un materiale molto più sicuro con un bagliore altrettanto efficace. In risposta, Blancpain utilizzò questo simbolo per indicare chiaramente che i suoi orologi erano sicuri da indossare. Questo esemplare, in ottimo stato di conservazione, è accompagnato da nostra certificazione di autenticità e un anno di garanzia di negozio sul funzionamento. Spedizioni in tutto il mondo con corriere assicurato Fedex
13cbb4d9e78b: Rarissimo Patek Philippe Calatrava in oro giallo 18kt, referenza 2526, del 1955. Introdotta nel 1952, liconica referenza 2526 rappresenta la prima grande innovazione in casa Patek Philippe, viene infatti equipaggiata dal primo movimento automatico, il famosissimo calibro 12-600. Per coronare il lancio del suo primo orologio automatico, la Patek optò per la realizzazione su una base d’argento di un quadrante in smalto di un inimitabile bianco crema. All’epoca la realizzazione di questi quadranti in smalto (unito alla necessità di forarne la delicata superficie, così da applicarvi gli indici) portò a una proporzione di circa 9 pezzi su 10 da scartare. Per ovviare alla difficoltà nella realizzazione, in seguito la Patek decise che gli indici sarebbero stati semplicemente incollati. Ciò ha comportato la classificazione di questi quadranti in Prima serie o Mark I (ovvero con indici applicati) e Seconda serie o Mark II(indici incollati), con i collezionisti che bramano in particolar modo la prima tipologia di quadranti di cui questo bellissimo esemplare è fornito!
